lessons.title: Cluster architecture in 3D

scenes.text: Kiran joins a platform team. Everyone talks about 'the API server' and 'kubelets'.
She explores a 3D model of a cluster.

steps.title: Control plane
steps.body:
- **kube-apiserver**: front door; every kubectl call goes here
- **etcd**: key-value store holding cluster state
- **kube-scheduler**: picks a node for each new pod
- **kube-controller-manager**: runs controllers that drive actual state to desired state

steps.title: Nodes
steps.body:
- **kubelet**: makes sure containers described in pod specs are running
- **container runtime** (e.g. containerd)
- **kube-proxy**: implements Service networking rules

steps.title: Desired state
steps.body: You declare what you want (YAML); controllers continuously reconcile reality toward it.

activity.prompt: Tap each component to learn its role. Explode the view to separate control plane from worker nodes.

objects.label: kube-apiserver
objects.info: The only component that talks to etcd. All clients and components communicate through it.

objects.label: etcd
objects.info: Consistent key-value store holding all cluster state. Back it up!

objects.label: kube-scheduler
objects.info: Assigns pending pods to nodes based on resources, affinity and taints.

objects.label: controller-manager
objects.info: Runs controllers such as Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers that reconcile desired state.

objects.label: worker node 1 (kubelet + containerd + kube-proxy)
objects.info: Runs pods. The kubelet reports status to the API server.

objects.label: worker node 2
objects.info: Another node; the scheduler spreads pods across nodes.

tour.text: Every kubectl command reaches the API server first.
The scheduler places new pods on nodes.

quiz.q: Which picks a node for a new pod?

story.title: Where does the DB password go?

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive config. Secrets hold sensitive data; by default they are only **base64-encoded**, not encrypted, so also enable encryption at rest and RBAC, or use an external secret manager.

lessons.title: Lab: CrashLoopBackOff

steps.title: Triage flow
steps.body:
1. `kubectl get pods` – status & restarts
2. `kubectl describe pod` – events, last state, exit code
3. `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` – logs from the crashed container
4. Fix config/image and verify

steps.title: --previous
steps.body: The current container may have just started; `--previous` shows why the last one died.

lessons.title: Lab: Pending pods

scenes.text: A new analytics deployment sits in Pending for 20 minutes.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Why Pending
steps.body:
- Insufficient CPU/memory on any node (requests too large)
- Taints without matching tolerations
- nodeSelector/affinity matching no node
- Unbound PersistentVolumeClaim

steps.title: Events say it
steps.body: '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory' tells you exactly why.

scenes.text: shop.example.com returns 503. Pods are Running and Ready.
Something between the Service and the pods is wrong.

steps.title: Selector mismatch
steps.body: A Service sends traffic to pods whose **labels** match its **selector**. If no pod matches, `kubectl get endpoints` (or endpointslices) shows none, and ingress returns 503.

terminal.prompt: Fix the Service selector so it matches the new pod label, then confirm endpoints exist.

responses.out: service/frontend patched

diagnosis.why: Endpoints empty; selector app=frontend vs label app.kubernetes.io/name.

resolution: Confirm pods are Ready and note their labels

closure.model: Root cause: frontend v5 changed pod labels to app.kubernetes.io/name=frontend but the Service selector stayed app=frontend, leaving zero endpoints; ingress returned 503. lessons.title: Lab: Roll back a failed upgrade

scenes.text: After upgrade to revision 7, frontend pods crash. Users see errors.
Rahul needs the last good release back in minutes.

steps.title: Rollback
steps.body: `helm history frontend` shows revisions; `helm rollback frontend 6` returns to the last good one. Use `--atomic` on upgrades so failed upgrades roll back automatically.

steps.title: Rollback is a new revision
steps.body: Helm records the rollback as a new revision number, keeping an audit trail.

steps.title: Data migrations
steps.body: Rolling back the app does not undo database migrations. Make migrations backward compatible.

lessons.title: Lab: Map checks to pipeline stages

story.title: Security at the end is too late

scenes.text: Security reviews happen a week before release and always find blockers.
Nikhil's team moves checks left into the pipeline.

steps.title: Typical checks
steps.body:
- **Pre-commit / PR**: secret scanning, linting, SAST (static code analysis)
- **Build**: SCA (dependency vulnerabilities & licences), SBOM generation
- **Image**: container image scanning, signing
- **Deploy**: policy checks (e.g. no privileged pods), IaC scanning
- **Runtime**: DAST, runtime detection, patching

steps.title: Fast feedback
steps.body: Run quick checks on every PR; run slow scans nightly but gate releases on critical findings.

ticket.short: Cloud access key exposed in public repository
ticket.description: Alert: AKIA… key for ci-deploy found in commit 4e5f6a7 on a public fork.

investigate.label: Check cloud audit logs for the key
investigate.reveal: Two calls from unknown IP 198.51.100.23 at 10:31: ListBuckets, RunInstances (denied).

investigate.label: Check key permissions
investigate.reveal: ci-deploy has broad EC2 and S3 permissions (over-privileged).

investigate.label: Ask developer to delete the commit only
investigate.reveal: Commit removed but key still valid; history and clones keep it.

diagnosis.q: What is the most urgent action?
diagnosis.why: Key is live and already used by an attacker.

resolution: Deactivate and delete the exposed key
Review audit logs for all actions by the key and contain any created resources
Rotate dependent secrets and move CI to OIDC short-lived credentials
Reduce ci-deploy permissions to least privilege
Add pre-commit secret scanning and record the incident

closure.model: Exposed ci-deploy key revoked at 10:38 (27 min after commit). Audit logs show ListBuckets and a denied RunInstances from 198.51.100.23; no resources created, no data accessed beyond listing. CI moved to OIDC federation; ci-deploy deleted; new role scoped to one bucket and one cluster. Pre-commit secret scanning enforced. Security review scheduled.

options: Key is still valid and copies exist

Prioritised above unexploited of same severity

rounds.q: Walk me through a CI/CD pipeline you would build for a containerised microservice.
points: push to registry with immutable tag
deploy to staging and smoke test
promote same artifact to prod with canary or approval
rounds.model: On every PR: lint, unit tests, SAST and secret scan. On merge: build the image once, tag it with the commit SHA, run SCA and image scans, push to the registry. Deploy to staging via Helm or GitOps, run smoke and integration tests, then promote the same image to production with a canary and automated rollback on SLO burn. Credentials come from OIDC, not static keys.
followups: How do you handle database migrations?

rounds.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you debug it?
points: describe for events and exit code
rounds.model: I'd run kubectl get pods to see restarts, kubectl describe pod to read events and the last exit code, then kubectl logs --previous for the crashed container. Exit 1 suggests an app or config error, 137 suggests OOM. I check ConfigMaps, Secrets and probes, fix the cause, roll out and verify the pod stays Ready.

rounds.q: How do you manage Terraform state in a team?
rounds.model: State lives in a remote backend with locking and encryption, access-restricted because it can contain secrets. Plans run in CI on every PR so reviewers see changes; applies run from the pipeline, not laptops. Modules keep environments consistent, and we detect drift with scheduled plans.
followups: How do you rename a resource safely?

rounds.q: Docker image is 1.5 GB. How would you shrink it?
rounds.model: Use a multi-stage build so the toolchain stays in the build stage, copy only the binary or app into a slim or distroless base, add a .dockerignore, install only runtime dependencies and clean package caches in the same layer. This also cuts the CVE count.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you automated something painful.
rounds.model: Our team restarted a stuck queue worker by hand about 24 times a week, around 6 hours of toil. I added a liveness check on consumer lag and an auto-remediation job, plus an alert if it fired more than 3 times an hour. Toil dropped to near zero and we found the real cause, a connection leak, through the alert data.
followups: How did you make sure the automation was safe?

tips: Mention verification and rollback in every answer

rounds.q: Our SLO is 99.9% monthly. How much downtime is that and how would you alert on it?
points: page fast burn ticket slow burn
rounds.model: 99.9% over 30 days gives an error budget of 0.1%, about 43.2 minutes of full outage or 0.1% of requests. I'd alert on burn rate with multiple windows: page if both 1 h and 5 min windows burn at around 14× (2% of the budget per hour), and ticket on slow burns such as 1× over three days.
followups: What if traffic is very low at night?

rounds.q: Latency doubled 10 minutes ago and nothing was deployed. Walk me through your response.
rounds.model: I'd declare an incident and assign roles, then check golden signals to see scope. Traces show which dependency got slower; I'd check config, feature-flag, infrastructure and third-party changes, since 'no deploy' doesn't mean nothing changed. Mitigate first: scale, fail over, shed or disable the feature. Keep stakeholders updated, then run a blameless postmortem.
followups: How do you decide to fail over regions?

rounds.q: Design a highly available URL shortener for 10,000 writes/s and 200,000 reads/s.
rounds.model: I'd confirm SLOs, say 99.95% availability and p99 read under 50 ms. Stateless API pods sit behind a load balancer across three zones. Short keys come from a pre-allocated ID range or a hash, avoiding a single global counter. Mappings are stored in a replicated key-value store, and a read-through cache plus CDN takes most of the read traffic. I'd add rate limiting, golden-signal dashboards, SLO burn alerts and capacity headroom of about 30%, then test zone failure.
followups: How do you handle a hot key?

rounds.q: Tell me about an incident you led and what changed afterwards.
rounds.model: A certificate rotation broke payments for 51 minutes. As incident commander I set up roles, made the call to roll back, and ran comms. In the blameless postmortem we found there was no pre-registration step with the acquirer. Actions were automated expiry checks and a staging handshake test. We have had no certificate incidents since.

tips: Always state assumptions and SLOs in design rounds

options: Check other changes (config, flags, infra, vendors)

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **SLI**: a measured ratio of good events to valid events (e.g. requests served < 300 ms ÷ all requests).
- **SLO**: a target for an SLI over a window (e.g. 99.9% over 28 days).
- **SLA**: a contract with consequences; usually looser than the SLO.

lessons.title: Lab: Compute the error budget

scenes.text: SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. Traffic: 50 million requests per 30 days.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Error budget
steps.body:
**Error budget = 1 − SLO.** For 99.9%: 0.1% may fail.

- Requests: 50,000,000 × 0.001 = **50,000 failed requests** allowed.
- Time (30 days = 43,200 min): 43,200 × 0.001 = **43.2 minutes** of full outage.

steps.title: Budget used
steps.body: If 20,000 requests failed so far: 20,000 ÷ 50,000 = 40% of budget used, 60% remaining.

lessons.title: Lab: Burn rates and alerts

scenes.text: Error rate jumped to 1.4% for the last hour. SLO is 99.9%.
Varun calculates the burn rate.

steps.title: Burn rate
steps.body: **Burn rate = observed error rate ÷ allowed error rate.** Burn rate 1 spends exactly the budget over the window. 1.4% ÷ 0.1% = **14×**.

steps.title: Time to exhaustion
steps.body: At 14× over a 30-day window, the whole budget lasts 30 ÷ 14 ≈ 2.14 days. One hour at 14× uses 14 ÷ 720 ≈ 1.94% of the monthly budget.

steps.title: Multi-window alerts
steps.body: A common pattern pages when both a long window (1 h) and short window (5 min) show a high burn rate (e.g. 14.4×), and tickets on slower burns (e.g. 1× over 3 days). The short window lets the alert reset quickly after recovery.

lessons.title: Lab: Train a perceptron by hand

scenes.text: An AND gate: output 1 only when both inputs are 1.
Update weights only on mistakes.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: ŷ = 1 if w·x + b > 0 else 0. For each example: w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x, b ← b + η(y − ŷ). Converges if the data are linearly separable (perceptron convergence theorem).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: η=1, w=(0,0), b=0. Example (1,1), y=1: ŷ=0 → w=(1,1), b=1. Example (0,0), y=0: z=1 → ŷ=1 → error −1 → w stays (1,1), b=0. Continue until all four are correct.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.body:
- Print intermediate values and compare with a hand calculation on a tiny example.
- Keep a fixed seed or fixed data while debugging.
- Re-run from a clean start before trusting the result.

lessons.title: Lab: XOR needs a hidden layer

scenes.text: XOR: 1 when inputs differ.
No single line separates the classes.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: XOR points (0,0),(1,1)→0 and (0,1),(1,0)→1: any line putting both 1s above leaves a 0 on the wrong side. A hidden layer composes OR and NAND: XOR = AND(OR(a,b), NAND(a,b)).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Hidden h1 = step(a+b−0.5) (OR), h2 = step(1.5−a−b) (NAND), output = step(h1+h2−1.5) (AND). For (1,0): h1=1,h2=1 → out step(0.5)=1 ✓. For (1,1): h2=0 → out 0 ✓.

steps.title: Check your work

- Print intermediate values and compare with a hand calculation on a tiny example.
- Keep a fixed seed or fixed data while debugging.
- Re-run from a clean start before trusting the result.

lessons.title: Lab: Backprop through one neuron by hand

scenes.text: A single sigmoid neuron with squared loss.
Chain rule flows from loss back to weights.

steps.title: Chain
steps.body: z = wx + b; a = σ(z); L = ½(a − y)². dL/da = a−y; da/dz = a(1−a); dz/dw = x. So dL/dw = (a−y)·a(1−a)·x.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Dropping the a(1−a) factor — the 'saturating' term that causes vanishing gradients.

steps.title: Deltas
steps.body: Output delta δ₂ = (a₂−y)·a₂(1−a₂). Hidden delta δ₁ = (W₂ᵀδ₂) ⊙ a₁(1−a₁). Gradients: dW₂ = δ₂a₁ᵀ, dW₁ = δ₁xᵀ; biases get the deltas.

lessons.title: Lab: SGD, momentum and Adam updates

scenes.text: A ravine-shaped loss: steep in one direction, shallow in another.
Momentum and adaptive rates help.

steps.title: Updates
steps.body: SGD: w ← w − ηg. Momentum: v ← βv + g; w ← w − ηv. Adam: m ← β₁m+(1−β₁)g; v ← β₂v+(1−β₂)g²; m̂=m/(1−β₁ᵗ); v̂=v/(1−β₂ᵗ); w ← w − η m̂/(√v̂+ε). Defaults β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=1e-8.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: First Adam step with g=2, η=0.1: m=0.2, v=0.004; m̂=2, v̂=4 → step = 0.1·2/2 = **0.1** — about η regardless of the gradient scale.

steps.title: Why bias correction
steps.body: m and v start at 0, so early estimates are biased low.

activity.prompt: Do 3 Adam steps with constant gradient g=2 and η=0.1 starting at w=1 and print w after each (5 d.p.).
activity.starter:

b1, b2, lr, eps, g = 0.9, 0.999, 0.1, 1e-8, 2.0
for t in range(1, 4):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g
    # TODO: bias-corrected moments
    w -= lr * mh / (sqrt(vh) + eps)
    print(round(w, 5))
activity.solution:
from math import sqrt
w, m, v = 1.0, 0.0, 0.0
b1, b2, lr, eps, g = 0.9, 0.999, 0.1, 1e-8, 2.0
for t in range(1, 4):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g
    mh, vh = m / (1 - b1 ** t), v / (1 - b2 ** t)
    w -= lr * mh / (sqrt(vh) + eps)
    print(round(w, 5))

steps.title: Dropout
steps.body: Training: keep each unit with prob p_keep, scale kept values by 1/p_keep (inverted dropout); testing: no dropout. **BatchNorm**: x̂=(x−μ_B)/√(σ²_B+ε), y=γx̂+β; at test time use running averages.

lessons.title: Lab: TF-IDF search engine

scenes.text: Three documents and a query.
Rare words matter more than common ones.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: TF = count(t,d)/|d|. IDF = ln(N/df) (a common variant; smoothed versions add 1). TF-IDF = TF·IDF. Rank documents by cosine between TF-IDF vectors.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: N=3 docs; 'the' appears in all → IDF = ln(3/3) = 0 (ignored). 'goal' appears in 1 → IDF = ln 3 = **1.0986**.

steps.title: Mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Bigram language model and perplexity

scenes.text: A phone keyboard suggests the next word.
Perplexity measures how surprised the model is.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: P(wᵢ|wᵢ₋₁) = (count(wᵢ₋₁wᵢ)+α)/(count(wᵢ₋₁)+α·V). Perplexity = exp(−(1/N)Σ ln P). Lower is better; a uniform model over V words has perplexity V.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Corpus: 'a b a b a c'. count(a)=3, count(a b)=2 → P(b|a)=2/3 (unsmoothed). Uniform over 10 words → perplexity 10.

steps.title: Add start tokens

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Output size = ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1. Conv parameters = (k·k·C_in + 1)·C_out. Pooling has no parameters. Receptive field grows with kernel size and stride.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: n=32, k=5, p=0, s=1 → 28. Parameters with C_in=3, C_out=6: (5·5·3+1)·6 = **456**. Then 2×2 max-pool stride 2 → 14×14×6.

steps.title: Mistake

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: r₀=1, j₀=1. For each layer: r ← r + (k−1)·j; j ← j·s. (r = receptive field, j = jump between neighbouring outputs.)

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Three 3×3 conv layers (stride 1): r = 1+2=3, 5, **7**. Two 3×3 convs equal one 5×5 receptive field with fewer parameters (2·9 vs 25 per channel pair).

steps.title: The first 10 minutes

- Trusting a column's name instead of its values.
- Treating 'NA', '-', '?', '' and 'null' as different things.

scenes.text: 30% of incomes are blank in a loan dataset.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body: **MCAR** (missing completely at random), **MAR** (depends on other observed columns), **MNAR** (depends on the missing value itself). Strategies: drop rows (only if few and MCAR), impute mean/median/mode, group-wise impute, add a **missing-indicator** column.

steps.title: Leakage
steps.body: Compute imputation values on the **training** set only, then reuse for test data.

courses.summary: Turn raw columns into model-ready features: standardisation, min-max, log transforms, one-hot and target encoding, binning, interaction and date features — with leakage-safe fitting.

lessons.title: Lab: Standardise, normalise and log-transform

scenes.text: Income is in lakhs, age in years — distance-based models get dominated by income.
Scaling puts features on comparable footing.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Standardise**: z=(x−μ)/σ (mean 0, sd 1). **Min-max**: (x−min)/(max−min) ∈[0,1]. **Log**: log(1+x) tames right skew. Tree models don't need scaling; kNN, SVM, k-means, neural nets and regularised linear models do.

steps.title: Leakage
steps.body: Compute μ, σ, min, max from **training** data and apply to test data — never refit on test.

activity.prompt: Fit mean and sd on train, then standardise train and test with those values (3 d.p.).

test = [25, 50]

sd = (sum((x - mu) ** 2 for x in train) / len(train)) ** 0.5
# TODO: use train statistics
print([z(x) for x in train], [z(x) for x in test])
activity.solution:
train = [10, 20, 30, 40]
test = [25, 50]
mu = sum(train) / len(train)
sd = (sum((x - mu) ** 2 for x in train) / len(train)) ** 0.5
z = lambda x: round((x - mu) / sd, 3)
print([z(x) for x in train], [z(x) for x in test])

lessons.title: Lab: One-hot and target encoding

scenes.text: Models can't read 'Pune'.

steps.title: Encoders
steps.body: **One-hot**: one 0/1 column per category (drop one to avoid collinearity). **Ordinal**: only if a true order exists (S<M<L). **Target encoding**: replace category by the mean target — powerful but leaky; use out-of-fold means with smoothing: (n·mean_cat + m·mean_global)/(n+m).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: City Pune target [1,0,1], Goa [0,0]. Global mean = 2/5 = 0.4. Smoothed Pune with m=2: (3·0.667 + 2·0.4)/5 = **0.56**.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Label-encoding cities as 0,1,2 makes distance models think Goa is 'between' Delhi and Pune.

class Pipe:
    def fit(self, rows):
        v = [r[0] for r in rows]

steps.title: MCC
steps.body: MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)), range −1..1; 0 = no better than chance. Balanced accuracy = (recall + specificity)/2.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 1000 transactions, 10 fraud. Model predicts all normal: TP=0, FN=10, FP=0, TN=990. Accuracy 99%; recall 0; balanced accuracy = (0+1)/2 = **0.5**; MCC = 0 (denominator 0 → defined as 0).

steps.title: Use several metrics
steps.body: No single number fits every problem.

steps.title: z-test
steps.body: p̂₁ = x₁/n₁, p̂₂ = x₂/n₂, pooled p̂ = (x₁+x₂)/(n₁+n₂). SE = √(p̂(1−p̂)(1/n₁+1/n₂)). z = (p̂₂ − p̂₁)/SE. |z| > 1.96 ⇒ p < 0.05 (two-sided).

steps.title: Peeking
steps.body: Checking the result daily and stopping when p<0.05 inflates false positives; fix the sample size in advance.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Per group n ≈ (z_α/2 + z_β)² [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] / (p₂−p₁)². With α=0.05 (z=1.96) and power 80% (z=0.84), (z_α/2+z_β)² = 7.85.

steps.title: Smaller effects cost more
steps.body: Halving the detectable lift quadruples the sample size.

The dot product measures how aligned their baskets are.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: For vectors a, b ∈ ℝⁿ: **a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ**. The **L2 norm** is ‖a‖ = √(a·a). The **L1 norm** is Σ|aᵢ|. Unit vector = a/‖a‖.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding instead of multiplying components.
- Forgetting the square root in the norm.
- Taking the dot product of vectors of different lengths (undefined).

activity.prompt: Compute a·b for a = (3, 0, 2) and b = (1, 4, 2).

lessons.title: Lab: Angle and cosine similarity

scenes.text: A search engine ranks documents by the angle between word-count vectors.
Small angle = similar content.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖). Value 1 means same direction, 0 orthogonal, −1 opposite. In text mining it is **cosine similarity**.

steps.title: Scale invariance
steps.body: Cosine ignores vector length: a document repeated twice has the same cosine with a query.

activity.prompt: Compute cosine similarity of (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6), and of (1, 0) and (0, 5); print 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
from math import sqrt
def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    # TODO: dot over product of norms
print(round(cos([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]), 4), round(cos([1, 0], [0, 5]), 4))
activity.solution:
from math import sqrt
def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (na * nb)
print(round(cos([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]), 4), round(cos([1, 0], [0, 5]), 4))
activity.hint: Work in small steps and print exactly what is asked.

quiz.q: Doubling a vector's length changes its cosine with others by…

lessons.title: Lab: Projection and independence

scenes.text: The shadow of a stick on the ground is a projection.
Projections underlie regression.

steps.title: Projection
steps.body: Projection of a onto b: **proj_b(a) = (a·b / b·b) b**. Scalar part = a·b/‖b‖. Vectors are **linearly independent** if no one is a combination of the others; in 2-D, (a₁,a₂),(b₁,b₂) are independent iff a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: a=(3,4), b=(1,0): a·b=3, b·b=1 → projection = (3,0). Residual (0,4) is orthogonal to b: (0,4)·(1,0)=0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by ‖b‖ instead of b·b for the vector form.
- Assuming perpendicular means independent only; any non-parallel pair is independent.

activity.prompt: Scalar projection of a = (3, 4) onto b = (4, 3): a·b/‖b‖.

quiz.why: Determinant 2·2 − 4·1 = 0, so one is a multiple of the other.

lessons.title: Lab: Matrix multiplication and shapes

story.title: One layer of a neural net

scenes.text: A layer maps 3 inputs to 2 outputs with a 2×3 weight matrix.
Shapes must match: (m×n)(n×p) = (m×p).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: (AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ Aᵢₖ Bₖⱼ. Inner dimensions must agree; the result has the outer dimensions. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: AB ≠ BA generally; it is associative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying element-wise (that is the Hadamard product).
- Ignoring shapes: (2×3)(2×3) is undefined.

activity.prompt: Write matmul(A, B) with nested loops and print A·B for A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]].
activity.starter:
def matmul(A, B):
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    # TODO: row-by-column sums
print(matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]))
activity.solution:
def matmul(A, B):
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(m)) for j in range(p)] for i in range(n)]
print(matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]))
activity.hint: Work in small steps and print exactly what is asked.

lessons.title: Lab: Determinant, inverse and linear systems

scenes.text: 2 coffees + 1 tea cost ₹70; 1 coffee + 3 teas cost ₹65.
The inverse solves it at once.

steps.title: 2×2 formulas
steps.body: For A=[[a,b],[c,d]]: det = ad − bc. If det ≠ 0, A⁻¹ = (1/det)[[d,−b],[−c,a]]. Solve Ax=y by x = A⁻¹y. det = 0 means singular: no unique solution.

activity.prompt: Solve 2c + t = 70 and c + 3t = 65. Enter the price of a coffee c.

lessons.title: Lab: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix

scenes.text: Some directions are only stretched, not turned, by a matrix.
PCA finds them in a covariance matrix.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Av = λv with v ≠ 0. Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0 → for 2×2: λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0. Sum of eigenvalues = trace; product = determinant.

steps.title: PCA link
steps.body: For a covariance matrix, the eigenvector with the biggest eigenvalue is the direction of maximum variance.

lessons.title: Lab: Derivative rules and numerical checks

scenes.text: Position s(t)=t² metres; speed is the derivative.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹; d/dx eˣ = eˣ; d/dx ln x = 1/x; (f+g)' = f'+g'; (cf)' = cf'; product rule (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Numerical: f'(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)]/(2h).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply by the exponent.
- Differentiating a constant to 1 (it is 0).
- Using a huge h (error) or tiny h (rounding).

steps.title: Gradient
steps.body: For f(x,y), ∂f/∂x treats y as constant. **∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)** points in the direction of steepest increase; descent moves along −∇f. At a minimum ∇f = 0.

lessons.title: Lab: Chain rule and the sigmoid

scenes.text: A neuron computes σ(wx+b); its loss depends on w through a chain.
The chain rule multiplies local derivatives.

steps.title: Chain rule
steps.body: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), dy/dx = f'(u)·g'(x). Sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) has σ'(z) = σ(z)(1−σ(z)). Maximum slope is 0.25 at z = 0.

steps.title: Vanishing gradients
steps.body: Deep sigmoid nets multiply many factors ≤ 0.25, so gradients shrink fast — one reason ReLU became popular.

lessons.title: Lab: The normal distribution and z-scores

steps.title: Normal
steps.body: z = (x−μ)/σ. Rule of thumb: 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ. Standard normal: P(Z<1)=0.8413, P(Z<1.5)=0.9332, P(Z<2)=0.9772.

steps.title: Python
steps.body: Φ(z) = 0.5(1 + erf(z/√2)) using math.erf.

lessons.title: Lab: Entropy and cross-entropy

scenes.text: A fair coin is more surprising than a biased one.
Entropy measures average surprise.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: H(p) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ (bits). Cross-entropy H(p,q) = −Σ pᵢ log qᵢ — the classification loss. KL(p‖q) = H(p,q) − H(p) ≥ 0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Fair coin: H = 1 bit. Biased 0.9/0.1: H = −0.9log₂0.9 − 0.1log₂0.1 = 0.1368+0.3322 = **0.469** bits. True label (1,0), prediction 0.8: CE = −ln 0.8 = 0.2231 nats.

steps.title: Pitfall
steps.body: log 0 is undefined; clip probabilities (e.g. 1e-12).

scenes.text: Group shoppers by spend and visits.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: 1) Choose k initial centres. 2) Assign each point to the nearest centre. 3) Move each centre to the mean of its points. 4) Repeat until assignments stop changing. It minimises inertia = Σ‖x − centre‖²; it finds a **local** optimum.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Points 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12 (1-D), centres 1 and 12. Assign: 10 is 9 from centre 1 and 2 from centre 12, so it joins 12. Clusters {1,2,3}, {10,11,12}; new centres 2 and 11; stable. Inertia = 2+2 = **4**.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Unscaled features.
- Assuming the result is unique (it depends on initial centres).

steps.title: Rows are strings

def pct(xs, p):
    s = sorted(xs)
    pos = (len(s) - 1) * p / 100
    lo = int(pos)
    hi = min(lo + 1, len(s) - 1)
    return s[lo] + (s[hi] - s[lo]) * (pos - lo)
x = [10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45]
q1, q3 = pct(x, 25), pct(x, 75)
iqr = q3 - q1

from math import sqrt
def pearson(x, y):
    mx, my = sum(x) / len(x), sum(y) / len(y)
    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    den = sqrt(sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x) * sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y))
    return num / den

lessons.title: Lab: Stationarity, differencing and ACF

story.title: Does the past predict the present?

scenes.text: A random walk wanders; its changes do not.
Autocorrelation reveals memory.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: A **stationary** series has constant mean, variance and autocovariance over time. First difference Δyₜ = yₜ − yₜ₋₁ removes a stochastic trend. ACF at lag k: rₖ = Σ(yₜ−ȳ)(yₜ₊ₖ−ȳ)/Σ(yₜ−ȳ)². For white noise rₖ ≈ 0, with 95% bounds ±1.96/√n.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: n=100 → bounds ±0.196: ACF values inside them are not significant.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Differencing too much adds spurious negative autocorrelation.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: yₜ = c + φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ. Stationary if |φ| < 1. Regress yₜ on yₜ₋₁ (simple regression). Forecast h steps: ŷ = μ + φʰ(yₜ − μ) where μ = c/(1−φ) — forecasts decay to the mean.

steps.title: Half-life
steps.body: Shock half-life = ln 0.5/ln φ ≈ 3.1 steps for φ=0.8.

lessons.title: Lab: Compute group fairness metrics

steps.title: Metrics
steps.body: **Demographic parity**: equal selection rate P(Ŷ=1|G). **Disparate impact ratio** = rate_B/rate_A (the US '80% rule' flags <0.8 as potential adverse impact). **Equal opportunity**: equal TPR across groups. **Equalised odds**: equal TPR and FPR. **Predictive parity**: equal precision.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Selection rates 0.40 vs 0.60 → ratio 0.667 < 0.8 → flag. TPR_A=0.80, TPR_B=0.60 → equal-opportunity gap 0.20.

steps.title: Not legal advice
steps.body: Legal thresholds differ by jurisdiction; treat the 80% rule as a screening heuristic.

lessons.title: Lab: Trade-offs and mitigation

scenes.text: Groups have different base rates.

steps.title: Impossibility
steps.body: When base rates differ between groups, a non-perfect classifier cannot satisfy calibration/predictive parity and equal FPR/FNR simultaneously (Kleinberg et al.; Chouldechova 2017). steps.title: k-anonymity
steps.body: A table is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifiers appears in at least k rows. Achieve by generalising (age 34 → 30–39, zip 560034 → 5600**) and suppressing rare rows. Limits: homogeneity attacks (all rows in a group share the same sensitive value) → l-diversity.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Groups (30–39,5600**): 3 rows; (40–49,5600**): 1 row → table is only **1-anonymous** (min group size 1).

steps.title: India

lessons.title: Lab: Differential privacy with the Laplace mechanism

scenes.text: Publish the number of patients with a rare condition without exposing any individual.
Add calibrated noise.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A mechanism M is ε-differentially private if for any two datasets differing in one person, P(M(D)∈S) ≤ e^ε P(M(D′)∈S). For a count (sensitivity 1) add Laplace noise with scale b = 1/ε. Smaller ε → stronger privacy, more noise. Noise standard deviation = √2·b.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ε=0.5 → b=2 → sd = 2.83. ε=0.1 → b=10 → sd = 14.1. Privacy budgets add up over repeated queries (composition).

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Answering unlimited queries with fresh noise lets an attacker average the noise away.

activity.prompt: Compute Laplace scale and noise standard deviation for ε = 1, 0.5, 0.1 (sensitivity 1) and the probability bound e^ε (3 d.p.).

for eps in (1, 0.5, 0.1):

activity.solution:
from math import exp, sqrt
for eps in (1, 0.5, 0.1):
    b = 1 / eps
    print(eps, b, round(sqrt(2) * b, 3), round(exp(eps), 3))

lessons.title: Lab: Permutation importance and Shapley values

story.title: Why did the model say no?

scenes.text: A customer asks why their loan was declined.
Explain with global and local methods.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Permutation importance**: shuffle one feature; importance = drop in score. **Shapley value** of feature i = average marginal contribution over all orderings (exact for few features). Local explanations support individual decisions; global ones support auditing.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Model f(x₁,x₂) = 3x₁ + 2x₂ + x₁x₂, baseline (0,0), instance (1,1): f=6. Shapley φ₁ = ½[(f(1,0)−f(0,0)) + (f(1,1)−f(0,1))] = ½[3 + 4] = **3.5**; φ₂ = ½[2 + 3] = 2.5; sum = 6 ✓ (efficiency).

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Correlated features make permutation importance misleading; explanations describe the model, not causes in the world.

lessons.title: What an ERP is and how SAP structures a company

scenes.text: At Contoso Foods, Sales keeps orders in one sheet, the warehouse keeps stock in another, and Finance keeps invoices in a third.
On month-end the three totals disagree and nobody knows which one is right.
The CFO approves an ERP project: one database, one version of the truth, shared by every department.

steps.title: ERP in one paragraph
steps.body: An **ERP** (Enterprise Resource Planning) system runs the core processes of a company on **one integrated database**: finance, purchasing, inventory, sales, production, HR. When the warehouse posts a goods receipt, the stock quantity, the inventory value in the books and the vendor liability all update from that single event.

steps.title: Organisational units you must know
steps.body:
- **Client**: the highest level, a self-contained unit with its own master data (usually one per system environment, e.g. client 100).
- **Company code**: the smallest unit for which a full legal set of books can be produced (one legal entity).
- **Plant**: a location that produces or stores goods (logistics).
- **Storage location**: a place inside a plant where stock is kept.
- **Purchasing organisation / sales organisation**: who buys, who sells.

steps.title: Finance building blocks
steps.body:
- **Chart of accounts**: the list of G/L accounts; assigned to company codes.
- **Fiscal year variant**: defines posting periods (e.g. April–March for India).
- **Posting key / document type**: tell the system debit or credit and the kind of document (e.g. vendor invoice).
- Every posting creates an **accounting document** where **total debits = total credits**.

steps.title: Worked example · a balanced document
steps.body:
Office rent of 40,000 plus 18% GST input tax is paid by bank.
- Rent expense debit: 40,000
- GST input tax debit: 40,000 × 0.18 = 7,200
- Bank credit: 40,000 + 7,200 = **47,200**

Debits 47,200 = credits 47,200, so the document can be posted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing **client** with **company code**: one client can hold many company codes.
- Thinking the ERP replaces process discipline; wrong master data produces wrong results quickly.
- Forgetting that a posting period must be open for the date you post.

tech-frontier-dimensions.description: Honest higher-dimensional maths: coordinates and distance in n-D, rotating hypercube and simplex projections from 4D to 8D, slices and shadows, the curse of dimensionality, and PCA with code and number-input labs.

lessons.title: Lab: Coordinates in more dimensions

scenes.text: Meera's game stores a character as (x, y, z, health, speed, armour, level, gold).
That's a point in 8-dimensional space: 8 independent numbers.

steps.title: Dimension = independent directions
steps.body: A line needs 1 number, a plane 2, space 3. Mathematically nothing stops us at 3: a point in ℝⁿ is just n numbers.

steps.title: 4D in maths vs physics
steps.body: In maths a 4th dimension is a fourth independent axis (w). In relativity, spacetime has 3 space + 1 time dimension, with a different geometry. We can't *see* 4D space, but we can calculate in it exactly.

steps.title: Honesty
steps.body: No screen or headset can show you a true 4D–8D world. We use projections (shadows), slices and numbers, and that is real maths.

courses.title: Seeing hypercubes from 4D to 8D
courses.summary: Build cubes dimension by dimension, count vertices, edges and faces with formulas and code, and explore rotating 4D–8D hypercube projections in 3D.
outcomes: Learners can build an n-cube by 'extruding' an (n−1)-cube

lessons.title: Explore the tesseract (4D)

scenes.text: Drag a point → segment; drag a segment → square; drag a square → cube.
Drag a cube in a 4th direction → tesseract.

steps.title: Extrusion rule
steps.body: Each step doubles the vertices and connects matching pairs. n-cube: 2ⁿ vertices, n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges, 2n facets ((n−1)-cubes).

steps.title: Tesseract
steps.body: 16 vertices, 32 edges, 24 square faces, 8 cubic cells.

steps.title: Reading the projection
steps.body: The familiar 'cube inside a cube' is a perspective projection: the inner cube is the far cell, not smaller in 4D. As it rotates in a 4D plane (like xw), cells appear to turn inside out; that's the projection, not the shape deforming.

activity.prompt: Rotate the 4D hypercube projection. Watch how the inner and outer cubes swap as it turns through 4D planes.

tour.text: 16 vertices: every combination of ±1 in 4 coordinates.
Each vertex connects to 4 others: 4 edges per vertex, 32 edges total.
The 'inner cube' is just the far cell in perspective.
Rotation in the xw-plane makes cells pass through each other in the shadow.

lessons.title: Lab: Count faces of any n-cube

scenes.text: How many squares does a 5-cube have?
Use C(n, k)·2ⁿ⁻ᵏ for k-dimensional faces.

steps.title: Why the formula works
steps.body: Pick which k of the n coordinates vary (C(n,k) ways) and fix each of the other n−k coordinates to one of 2 values (2ⁿ⁻ᵏ).

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Euler characteristic: alternating sum of face counts (excluding the whole cell) of a convex polytope's boundary is 1 − (−1)ⁿ: 2 for 3D, 0 for 4D.

activity.prompt: Read n and print the number of k-faces of the n-cube for k = 0 … n.
activity.starter:
from math import comb
n = int(input())
# TODO: number of k-dimensional faces of the n-cube is C(n, k) * 2^(n-k), for k = 0..n
print("")
activity.solution:
from math import comb
n = int(input())
print(" ".join(str(comb(n, k) * 2 ** (n - k)) for k in range(n + 1)))
activity.hint: comb(n, k) * 2**(n - k)

steps.title: What you see

steps.title: Interpretation

lessons.title: Lab: Where did the volume go?

scenes.text: A ball fits snugly inside a unit cube. In 2D it fills 78.5% of the square; in 3D, 52.4%.
In 8D, less than 2%.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Volume of an n-ball of radius r: πⁿᐟ² / Γ(n/2 + 1) · rⁿ. With r = ½ inside the unit cube.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Most of a high-dimensional cube's volume is in the corners, far from the centre. Random points become far apart and sparse.

activity.prompt: Print the volume of the ball of radius ½ for n = 1 … 8 (4 decimals).

import math
for n in range(1, 9):
    v = 0  # TODO: volume of the ball of radius 1/2 in n dimensions: pi^(n/2) / Gamma(n/2 + 1) * (1/2)^n
    print(n, f"{v:.4f}")
activity.solution:
import math
for n in range(1, 9):

steps.title: PCA in words
steps.body: Centre (and usually standardise) the data → compute the covariance matrix → its eigenvectors are the principal directions, eigenvalues their variances → keep the top k.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Eigenvalues 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.5 (total 8). PC1 explains 50%; PC1+PC2 = 75%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to standardise features with different units
- Interpreting PCs as real causes; they're directions of variance

lessons.title: Lab: 2×2 PCA by formula

scenes.text: Standardised height and weight have covariance matrix [[3, 1], [1, 1]] in some toy units.
Find the eigenvalues by formula.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: λ₁ + λ₂ = trace = a + c; λ₁·λ₂ = determinant = ac − b².

activity.prompt: Read a, b, c of a 2×2 covariance matrix. Print both eigenvalues and PC1's share of variance.
activity.starter:
import math
a, b, c = map(float, input().split())   # covariance matrix [[a, b], [b, c]]
# TODO: eigenvalues are (a+c)/2 +/- sqrt(((a-c)/2)^2 + b^2); print both and PC1's share of variance
l1 = l2 = 1.0
print(f"{l1:.4f} {l2:.4f} {l1 / (l1 + l2):.4f}")
activity.solution:
import math
a, b, c = map(float, input().split())
m = (a + c) / 2
r = math.sqrt(((a - c) / 2) ** 2 + b ** 2)
l1, l2 = m + r, m - r
print(f"{l1:.4f} {l2:.4f} {l1 / (l1 + l2):.4f}")

lessons.title: Lab: Choose k for 95% variance

scenes.text: Keep enough components to retain 95% of the variance.
Use cumulative sums of sorted eigenvalues.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Sort eigenvalues descending, add them up, stop when the cumulative share reaches the target.

steps.title: Scree plot
steps.body: Plot eigenvalues; an 'elbow' suggests a natural k. Also consider the downstream task.

activity.prompt: Read eigenvalues and print the smallest k reaching 95% cumulative variance.
activity.starter:
ev = list(map(float, input().split()))
target = 0.95
# TODO: sort eigenvalues descending, add them up until the cumulative share reaches 95%, print k
print(0)
activity.solution:
ev = list(map(float, input().split()))
target = 0.95
total = sum(ev)
cum = 0
for k, e in enumerate(sorted(ev, reverse=True), start=1):
    cum += e
    if cum / total >= target - 1e-12:
        print(k)
        break
activity.hint: Sort descending; cum += e; if cum/total >= 0.95: print(k)

steps.title: ADC basics
steps.body: An n-bit ADC splits 0…Vref into 2ⁿ steps. 10-bit at 3.3 V: one step ≈ 3.22 mV.

lessons.title: Lab: Voltage dividers and battery life

scenes.text: A 2,000 mAh battery, a node that sleeps at 0.01 mA and wakes at 80 mA for 2 s every 10 minutes.
How many days?

steps.title: Average current
steps.body: I_avg = (I_active·t_active + I_sleep·t_sleep)/period. Here: (80 × 2 + 0.01 × 598)/600 ≈ 0.277 mA.

steps.title: Life
steps.body: 2,000 mAh / 0.277 mA ≈ 7,220 h ≈ 300 days (ignoring self-discharge and temperature).

steps.title: Voltage divider
steps.body: Vout = Vin × R2/(R1+R2). To read a 6 V battery on a 3.3 V ADC use e.g. R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ → 3 V.

lessons.title: Lab: Publish and subscribe with MQTT

scenes.text: The dashboard shows no readings from field 2.

steps.title: MQTT
steps.body: Lightweight publish/subscribe over TCP. Clients publish to topics (farm/field1/temp); the broker forwards to subscribers. Wildcards: + (one level), # (all below). Default port 1883; 8883 for TLS.

steps.title: QoS
steps.body: 0: at most once · 1: at least once (duplicates possible) · 2: exactly once (more overhead). Retained messages give new subscribers the last value.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Topic typos (case-sensitive)
- Leading slash '/farm' is a different topic
- No authentication on a public broker

lessons.title: Lab: Forward kinematics of a 2-link arm

scenes.text: A pick-and-place arm has two 1 m links.
Given joint angles, compute the gripper position.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: x = L1 cos θ1 + L2 cos(θ1 + θ2), y = L1 sin θ1 + L2 sin(θ1 + θ2).

steps.title: Inverse kinematics
steps.body: Going from a desired (x, y) to angles is harder: there may be two solutions (elbow up/down) or none if out of reach.

activity.prompt: Read L1 L2 θ1 θ2 (degrees) and print the end-effector x and y.

import math
L1, L2, t1, t2 = map(float, input().split())   # link lengths and joint angles in degrees
# TODO: x = L1 cos t1 + L2 cos(t1+t2), y = L1 sin t1 + L2 sin(t1+t2)  (use radians!)
x = y = 0.0
print(f"{round(x, 4) + 0.0:.4f} {round(y, 4) + 0.0:.4f}")
activity.solution:
import math
L1, L2, t1, t2 = map(float, input().split())
a, b = math.radians(t1), math.radians(t1 + t2)
x = L1 * math.cos(a) + L2 * math.cos(b)
y = L1 * math.sin(a) + L2 * math.sin(b)
print(f"{round(x, 4) + 0.0:.4f} {round(y, 4) + 0.0:.4f}")
activity.hint: Convert degrees with math.radians before cos/sin.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body: v = (v_R + v_L)/2, ω = (v_R − v_L)/b, where b is the wheel separation.

steps.title: Spin in place

scenes.text: The robot must stop at 10 m.

steps.title: PID
steps.body: u = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt + Kd·de/dt. P reacts to current error, I removes steady-state error, D damps overshoot.

steps.title: Toy P-loop
steps.body: Kp = 2, each step pos += 0.1·u. Error shrinks by 20% each step: after 5 steps pos = 10(1 − 0.8⁵) ≈ 6.723.

steps.title: Tuning
steps.body: Too high Kp → oscillation; too low → sluggish. Tune step by step, with safety limits.

activity.prompt: Simulate 5 steps of a proportional controller and print the final position.
activity.starter:
kp = 2.0
target, pos = 10.0, 0.0
for step in range(5):
    # TODO: error = target - pos; u = kp * error; pos moves by 0.1 * u
    pass
print(f"{pos:.3f}")
activity.solution:
kp = 2.0
target, pos = 10.0, 0.0
for step in range(5):
    error = target - pos
    u = kp * error
    pos += 0.1 * u
print(f"{pos:.3f}")
activity.hint: error = target - pos; u = kp*error; pos += 0.1*u

lessons.title: Lab: Shannon capacity

scenes.text: Capacity C = B·log₂(1 + SNR).
Double the bandwidth → double the capacity; double the SNR → only a bit more.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: B in Hz, SNR as a ratio (not dB). 30 dB = 1000.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: B = 100 MHz, SNR = 1000: C = 10⁸ × log₂(1001) ≈ 10⁸ × 9.97 ≈ 997 Mbit/s (theoretical limit for one stream).

steps.title: dB
steps.body: SNR(dB) = 10·log₁₀(SNR). 20 dB = 100.

activity.prompt: B = 20 MHz and SNR = 100 (20 dB). Shannon capacity in Mbit/s? (log₂101 ≈ 6.658)

steps.title: 5G service types
steps.body: eMBB (enhanced mobile broadband), URLLC (ultra-reliable low latency, e.g. industrial control), mMTC (massive IoT). Network slicing gives virtual networks with different guarantees.

lessons.title: Lab: Cold-chain monitor for vaccines

scenes.text: A clinic stores vaccines that must stay between 2 and 8 °C.
Design a monitor that alerts staff.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Two sensors (redundancy) → microcontroller → Wi-Fi/cellular → MQTT over TLS → alert by SMS/app if outside 2–8 °C for over 5 minutes; local buzzer if offline.

steps.title: Avoid false alarms
steps.body: Require the reading to stay out of range for a few minutes (door openings cause brief spikes).

steps.title: Life-critical
steps.body: Alerts must reach a human; test the escalation path monthly.

activity.prompt: Order the cold-chain alert logic
items: Read both temperature sensors every 30 s
Compare readings; flag a sensor fault if they disagree by > 1 °C
If temperature is outside 2–8 °C, start a timer
If still outside after 5 minutes, sound the buzzer and publish an alert
Escalate by SMS to the duty pharmacist
Log the event with times for the audit

lessons.title: Lab: Troubleshoot the incident

scenes.text: The clinic says the fridge warmed overnight but no alert arrived.
Investigate like a support engineer.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Gather facts → check each hop (sensor, node, network, broker, alert service) → find root cause → fix → verify → prevent.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: Build a timeline from logs before guessing.

steps.title: Red herrings
steps.body: The first suspicious thing isn't always the cause.

ticket.short: Fridge got warm overnight, no alert received
ticket.description: Morning staff found fridge at 11 °C. Nobody got any SMS. The little device on the fridge has a green light. Please check urgently, we had to quarantine stock.
worknotes: Stock quarantined per SOP by pharmacy.

investigate.label: Check broker logs for node-03
investigate.reveal: node-03 published readings all night; values rose above 8 °C at 01:40.

investigate.label: Check the alert service logs
investigate.reveal: 01:46 alert generated → SMS gateway returned 'ERR 402: insufficient credit'.

investigate.label: Ask staff to restart the node
investigate.reveal: Node restarts fine; readings resume. Doesn't explain the missing SMS.

investigate.label: Check Wi-Fi signal at the fridge

options: The SMS gateway account ran out of credit, so alerts failed to send
diagnosis.why: Data and alert generation worked; delivery failed at the SMS provider.

resolution: Top up the SMS account and send a test alert
Add a second alert channel (app push or voice call)
Add monitoring on the SMS gateway's error responses and credit balance
Document the incident and update the runbook
Confirm with the pharmacy that test alerts arrive

closure.model: Root cause: SMS gateway credit exhausted; alert generated at 01:46 but rejected (ERR 402). Fix: credit topped up, test alert received by duty pharmacist at 10:20. Prevention: second channel (app push) added, low-credit and send-failure alerts configured, runbook updated.
